Cold Chain Logistics Market Overview
The global cold chain logistics market is projected to experience significant growth, with its market size estimated at USD 490,576.32 million in 2026. The market is expected to reach USD 1,800,560.55 million by 2035, expanding at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15.3% during the forecast period. This growth is anticipated to be driven by rising demand for temperature-controlled transportation, expanding food and pharmaceutical industries, technological advancements, and increasing global trade.
The cold chain logistics market supports temperature-controlled storage, transportation, handling, and distribution of perishable products across international and domestic supply chains. Refrigerated warehouses, reefer vehicles, insulated containers, monitoring sensors, and warehouse automation protect product quality from production through final delivery. Food and beverages represent the leading application segment because dairy, meat, seafood, frozen foods, and fresh produce require controlled environments. Roadways represent the leading transportation mode due to flexible routing and last-mile accessibility. Market operators increasingly deploy internet-connected sensors, automated storage systems, predictive maintenance, and natural refrigerants to reduce temperature excursions, energy consumption, product loss, and regulatory risk.
The United States cold chain logistics market is supported by a large food-processing sector, extensive grocery distribution networks, pharmaceutical manufacturing, and growing consumption of frozen products. Operators serve more than 330 million consumers through refrigerated warehouses, food production sites, ports, distribution centers, hospitals, and retail outlets. Road transportation remains essential because temperature-sensitive shipments must move between farms, processors, storage facilities, supermarkets, restaurants, and healthcare locations. Domestic providers are expanding automated high-bay warehouses, port-adjacent import hubs, and real-time temperature monitoring. The country also faces aging refrigeration infrastructure, electricity-cost pressure, driver availability constraints, strict food-safety requirements, and uneven cold-storage availability outside major logistics corridors.
Key Findings
 Market Size and Forecast: The market reached USD 490576.32 Million in 2026 and is forecast at USD 1800560.55 Million by 2035, recording 15.3% CAGR.
 Type Leadership: Roadways lead with 58% market share, supported by route flexibility, extensive reefer fleets, regional distribution, and essential last-mile connectivity.
 Application Leadership: Food and beverages account for 76% share as frozen food, dairy, meat, seafood, and produce require uninterrupted temperature control.
 Key Company Landscape: Lineage Logistics and Americold Logistics lead through extensive warehouse networks, automated facilities, integrated transportation, and technology-supported inventory management.
 Fastest Growing Region: Asia leads with 38% share, driven by urbanization, food exports, pharmaceutical production, modern retail, and refrigerated infrastructure investment.
 Key Trends: Connected monitoring and automation are expanding, while electricity costs and temperature excursions challenge operators managing increasingly complex distribution networks.

Cold Chain Logistics Market Latest Trends
The cold chain logistics market is moving toward connected, automated, and energy-efficient operations. Internet-connected temperature sensors provide continuous cargo visibility across refrigerated warehouses, vehicles, aircraft, vessels, and last-mile delivery routes. Operators increasingly connect sensor information with transportation management and warehouse management platforms, enabling faster intervention when temperature, humidity, door status, or equipment performance moves outside permitted conditions. Automated storage and retrieval systems are gaining importance because they increase storage density and reduce employee exposure to freezing environments. Roadways retain 58% of market activity, encouraging investment in telematics, electric refrigeration units, route optimization, and predictive fleet maintenance.
Artificial intelligence supports demand forecasting, pallet positioning, labor scheduling, compressor management, and refrigeration-load balancing. Digital documentation is also replacing manual records as food producers and healthcare companies seek auditable custody histories. Sustainability has become a central procurement requirement. Cold-storage operators are adopting rooftop solar systems, battery storage, improved insulation, low-emission refrigerants, and heat-recovery equipment. Food and beverages generate 76% of demand, making waste reduction a critical commercial priority. Additional trends include port-based refrigerated hubs, shared-user warehouses, pharmaceutical qualification programs, micro-fulfillment facilities, and multimodal services. However, cybersecurity exposure, fragmented data standards, capital intensity, and electricity-price volatility continue affecting deployment decisions.
Cold Chain Logistics Market Dynamics
DRIVER
"Rising demand for safe temperature-controlled food and healthcare distribution."
Demand for frozen foods, dairy products, meat, seafood, fresh produce, vaccines, biologics, and specialty medicines is increasing the operational importance of cold chain logistics. Food and beverages account for 76% of market demand because product freshness, shelf life, and microbiological safety depend on controlled handling. Urban consumers expect wider product availability, faster delivery, and consistent quality across supermarkets, restaurants, convenience stores, and online grocery platforms. Healthcare manufacturers similarly require validated lanes, qualified packaging, calibrated sensors, and documented chain-of-custody procedures. These conditions encourage investment in refrigerated warehouses, reefer vehicles, airport pharmaceutical stations, port facilities, and regional distribution centers. Exporters also need certified infrastructure to satisfy destination-market safety requirements. Operators capable of combining storage, transportation, customs support, packaging, and digital monitoring are receiving greater preference from customers seeking fewer handoffs and stronger accountability.
RESTRAINT
"High infrastructure, refrigeration, energy, and maintenance requirements."
Cold chain logistics requires specialized buildings, insulated loading areas, refrigeration equipment, backup power, reefer fleets, monitoring instruments, and trained personnel. These assets cost more to operate than ambient logistics infrastructure because temperature must remain stable throughout storage and movement. Refrigeration systems consume substantial electricity, while fuel use affects road-based distribution expenses. Roadways hold 58% of market activity, making diesel prices, driver wages, vehicle maintenance, and refrigeration-unit servicing important cost variables. Smaller providers can struggle to finance automation, modern refrigerants, generator capacity, and cybersecurity systems. Utilization also changes with harvesting cycles, retail promotions, and seasonal food demand, creating periods of unused capacity. Older warehouses may require costly insulation upgrades or equipment replacement. Regulatory audits, calibration, sanitation, insurance, and product-liability exposure add further expense, limiting entry and slowing infrastructure development in underserved markets.
OPPORTUNITY
"Expansion of automated regional facilities and integrated multimodal networks."
Large opportunities exist in emerging cities, agricultural production areas, pharmaceutical clusters, border crossings, seaports, and airport cargo zones where temperature-controlled capacity remains insufficient. Asia represents 38% of the cold chain logistics market, supported by food exports, modern retail development, healthcare manufacturing, and urban consumption. Investors can establish multi-temperature facilities capable of storing frozen, chilled, and controlled-room-temperature products within a single location. Automated high-bay warehouses provide additional opportunity by increasing pallet density, lowering heat infiltration, and improving inventory accuracy. Operators can also develop control-tower services that connect warehouse, vehicle, vessel, customs, and delivery data. Shared-user networks are attractive to smaller manufacturers that cannot support dedicated infrastructure. Other opportunities include reusable thermal packaging, solar-powered refrigeration, battery-supported warehouses, pharmaceutical airfreight services, and cross-border food corridors. Partnerships among ports, rail operators, warehouse providers, and technology companies can reduce transfer delays and strengthen end-to-end visibility.
CHALLENGE
"Maintaining uninterrupted temperature integrity across fragmented supply chains."
A shipment can pass through farms, processing plants, warehouses, customs facilities, ports, airports, vehicles, retail distribution centers, and last-mile carriers before reaching its destination. Every transfer creates exposure to door openings, incorrect handling, refrigeration failure, delays, sensor gaps, or documentation errors. Healthcare products can have narrow approved temperature conditions, while food categories require separate frozen, chilled, and humidity-controlled environments. The market’s 13% airways share carries particularly time-sensitive and high-value goods, increasing the consequences of airport delays or capacity shortages. Fragmented technology systems make it difficult to establish a unified shipment record. Cyberattacks can interrupt warehouse management, transport scheduling, and inventory release. Additional challenges include technician shortages, inconsistent electricity supply, border congestion, extreme weather, and limited reefer availability. Providers must combine contingency planning, backup equipment, employee training, validated packaging, calibrated monitoring, and rapid exception management to protect product integrity.
Cold Chain Logistics Market Segmentation
Cold chain logistics market segmentation reflects transportation speed, shipment value, route length, temperature sensitivity, and distribution requirements. By type, the market comprises roadways, seaways, and airways. Roadways dominate domestic and regional delivery, seaways support large international cargo volumes, and airways serve urgent or high-value shipments. By application, the market includes food and beverages, healthcare, and other applications. Each segment requires different packaging, monitoring, validation, handling, and documentation procedures. Providers increasingly combine these categories through multimodal networks and multi-temperature storage facilities.

CAN BRITAIN’S COLD CHAIN STAND THE HEAT?
ACCOMMODATING YOUR FUTURE Exploring what changing demand and evolving operational pressures mean for the UK’s temperature-controlled logistics network.
A FUTURE SPACE FOCUS REPORT In the year that marked the UK’s hottest summer on record, the resilience of the nation’s cold chain has become a headline topic. Rising temperatures have brought greater attention to the economic and operational pressures facing the network, highlighting both its significance and its potential vulnerabilities.
Despite being a relatively niche logistics subsector, the cold chain is vital infrastructure. Temperature-controlled storage and transportation networks underpin around half of the nation’s food supply and a significant proportion of its pharmaceutical distribution. Highly specialised logistics facilities form a critical part of this network, providing the controlled environments needed to safely store products and support their movement through the supply chain. The importance of a resilient cold chain is clear: disruption can directly affect food availability, the supply of essential healthcare products and wider economic activity.
Against this backdrop, this report examines the expanding and changing demands being placed on the cold chain, from evolving consumer habits and growth across temperature-sensitive product categories to the changing climate and increasingly complex operational requirements.
We consider whether the logistics real estate supporting the UK’s cold chain is equipped not only for today’s needs, but also those of the future, and how occupiers can prepare and respond through informed decision-making around location, power, building specification and adaptability.
Approximately 49% of food and beverages produced and sold by UK manufacturers, valued at £50 billion, consists of chilled or frozen products.1 Around one-fifth (£2.7 billion) of pharmaceutical products produced and sold by UK manufacturers require cold chain logistics.2 The cold chain directly adds £14bn in gross value to the UK economy each year, supporting 184,000 jobs and contributing £3.7bn in tax revenue.3 There are around 500 major cold stores in the UK, from smaller cross-docking operations and local delivery points up to 47-metre-high automated units capable of storing over 150,000 pallets of frozen and chilled products.4 INTRODUCTION Cold storage is a highly specialised market, with several periods over the last five years alone demonstrating how quickly disruption and changing supply chain requirements can impact available space.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Cold Chain Federation reported that the UK effectively ran out of available long-term cold storage as disruption to established product flows placed acute pressure on capacity. CoStar recorded vacancy at just 0.7% in late 20225 and changes to post-Brexit ordering requirements, which created uncertainty around the timing of imports and exports, also brought the network close to capacity on several further occasions.6 While recent data points to a gradual increase in cold storage vacancy rates, partially driven by speculative development of pharmaceutical-focused space, it remains a relatively small and specialised subsector, meaning a few individual buildings can have an outsized impact on the headline vacancy rate. The significant shifts in availability seen in recent years highlight a broader question around preparedness. This is particularly relevant within the UK food system, which has historically been geared towards efficiency. Defra’s UK Food Security Report 2024 stresses the prevalence of just-in-time models and low stockholding among many UK businesses, which can compound the impact of single points of failure within the supply chain.7 Long-term capacity requirements therefore need to account not only for demand under normal operating conditions, but the ability of cold chain networks to respond to future shocks. This does not necessarily mean simply holding more stock or providing more space; resilience depends on having sufficient capacity, flexibility and supporting infrastructure in the right places when it is needed.
PART 1: The cold chain under pressure Looking further ahead, a growing population will increase the underlying requirement for food and other temperature-sensitive products. The Office for National Statistics projects that the UK population will expand by 7.3%, or 4.9 million people, from 2022 levels to mid-2032.8 The relationship between population growth and cold storage requirements will not be linear, as improvements in forecasting, inventory management and supply-chain efficiency enable existing capacity to be used more effectively. However, it is not only the number of consumers that is changing; the UK’s demographic profile, the way people shop, what they eat, and their lifestyle choices are evolving too.
Modern consumers expect convenient and seamless access to food throughout the day, 365 days a year. The traditional supermarket shop has been supplemented by home deliveries, convenience stores and direct-to-customer services, increasing the number of routes through which temperature-controlled products now need to travel, creating demand for more complex, and in some cases more localised, cold chain networks.
Alongside these increased routes to market, shifts in established categories and the emergence of new temperature-sensitive products are broadening cold chain requirements. Three areas illustrate how changing consumer preferences are translating into evolving demands on temperature-controlled logistics: PART 2: Demand is expanding and changing FROZEN DEMAND TEMPERATURE-CONTROLLED PHARMACEUTICALS HUMAN-GRADE PET FOOD Frozen foods experienced a significant uplift in retail value following the pandemic and subsequent cost-of-living pressures, with UK sales reaching £8.5 billion in the year to March 2024, almost 12% higher than the previous year. More recent data suggests this elevated level of spending has been sustained: the market reached £8.8 billion in the 52 weeks to November 2025. Over this later period, sales value increased 2% year-on-year.9 While overall unit sales softened by 0.4%, demand continues to evolve across the category, with frozen snacks recording 11% value growth and 6.9% unit growth, and handheld ice cream increasing 8.6% in value and 1.6% in units.10 For cold chain operators, this changing product mix reinforces the importance of flexible infrastructure capable of adapting as demand shifts between product categories. Earlier this year, Farmfoods, the British supermarket chain specialising in frozen produce, committed to three units totalling around 800,000 sq ft in Daventry. Taken on a considerable 25-year lease, the facilities will support frozen and ambient storage, transportation and recycling as the retailer expands its UK operations.11 The scale and duration of the commitment demonstrate how long-term business growth can translate into significant logistics requirements, while highlighting the value of sites capable of accommodating future expansion.
FROZEN DEMAND TEMPERATURE-CONTROLLED PHARMACEUTICALS The cold chain plays a critical role in the storage and distribution of certain medicines and vaccines. Across the pharmaceutical network, Good Distribution Practice (GDP) standards govern the storage, handling and transportation of medicines under appropriate conditions, helping to maintain their quality and integrity throughout the supply chain.
The critical role of temperature-controlled infrastructure was brought into sharp focus during the COVID-19 pandemic, when the urgent vaccine rollout created highly specialised requirements across the cold chain. EVOLVING PRODUCT MIX (year to November 2025) FROZEN SNACKS 11% value growth 6.9% unit growth HANDHELD ICE CREAMS 8.6% value growth 1.6% unit growth The Pfizer/BioNTech vaccine, for example, initially required storage between -60°C and -80°C, prompting the NHS to quickly establish transport routes and vaccination hubs capable of managing ultra-low-temperature storage and distribution.12 The experience demonstrated the importance of preparedness and adaptable infrastructure: pharmaceutical innovation can rapidly create new cold storage and distribution requirements that existing networks must be able to accommodate. More recently, the rising popularity of GLP-1 medications (which mimic a natural gut hormone to help lower blood sugar and reduce appetite) demonstrates how pharmaceutical innovation and a consumer trend can have a ripple effect across the cold chain. The doubling in usage among UK consumers in just nine months from 3.1% in June 2025 to 6% in March 2026 has created rapid requirements for pharmaceutical storage and distribution while simultaneously affecting food consumption and product development.13 As many injectable GLP-1 medications require temperature-controlled handling and distribution, growing adoption is contributing to increased requirements for specialist pharmaceutical logistics globally. In June 2026, UPS announced a $48 million investment in 27 temperature-controlled facilities across Europe, Asia and the Americas, citing GLP-1 injectables as a significant driver.14 Investment in UK-specific pharmaceutical cold chain infrastructure is also emerging: in June 2026, GEODIS opened a new temperature-controlled, GDP-compliant pharmaceutical warehouse in Manchester, providing 2,000 pallet positions.15 Rapid GLP-1 adoption forms part of a wider shift towards increasingly sophisticated, temperature-sensitive medicines, which are directly available to consumers outside of NHS pathways, creating new requirements for specialist healthcare logistics infrastructure in the UK.
The food-market implications of growing GLP-1 adoption are more nuanced. Users typically consume less food volume overall, potentially reducing demand for some food categories, but changing eating habits are also prompting product innovation around smaller, more protein-dense and nutrient-rich meals. In January 2026, Morrisons launched a 53-product Applied Nutrition range, including seven portion-controlled ready meals developed with GLP-1 users in mind, while Co-op introduced four 250g mini meals for consumers with smaller appetites, not replacing larger portion sizes, but adding to the category. In July, Fit Foods launched a further five-product Mini Meals range across 450 Tesco stores.16 These new ranges illustrate how healthcare innovation can translate into new food SKUs and formats moving through temperature-controlled supply chains, potentially adding complexity to storage, picking and fulfilment requirements.
Pharmaceutical innovation can rapidly create new cold storage and distribution requirements that existing networks must be able to accommodate.
HUMAN-GRADE PET FOOD The nation’s cold chain is not only made up of human consumables and pharmaceuticals. Cold Chain Logistics: Key Challenges and Strategies
Listen to this post about Cold chain: Challenges and strategies in the distribution of perishable goods here.
5:58
The cold chain is the uninterrupted sequence of temperature-controlled storage and transportation logistics processes required to preserve food safety and quality from origin to final delivery. In Latin America, diverse geography, variable climates, and long distances in the field make temperature management a highly strategic and essential process to mitigate biological and operational risks.
What is Cold Chain Logistics?
Cold Chain Logistics is an intricate and vital process, central to the preservation and safe transport of temperature-sensitive products. It includes a comprehensive system involving refrigerated transport methods, such as trucks, ships, and airplanes, as well as cold storage facilities. The primary goal is to maintain a constant temperature range, ensuring the quality and safety of the products from the point of origin to the destination.
Executive Summary
Maintaining an uninterrupted cold chain in Latin America represents a critical challenge for protecting high-value food items and supplies for the HORECA and Foodservice industries. Temperature deviations en route and operational delays often cause significant inventory losses and delivery rejections. Implementing a TMS (Transport Management System that centralizes planning and execution logistics) helps companies overcome these challenges by integrating satellite visibility, real-time monitoring, and automated alerts, achieving a reduction of up to 30% in transportation costs and distribution incidents for perishable goods.
What are the main challenges in the cold chain and how does a TMS solve them?
Distributing refrigerated and frozen food involves managing multiple variables in transit. From traffic congestion and unscheduled stops to constant vehicle door openings, cargo is exposed to temperature fluctuations that can compromise sensory quality and food safety.
Below is an analysis of the primary challenges in cold chain logistics alongside the technological solutions offered by a specialized platform:
|  |  |  |
 --- 
| Operational Challenge | Impact on Cargo | Solution with a TMS |
| Temperature deviations en route | Alteration of food properties, increased bacterial risk, partial or total loss of high-value supplies, and regulatory non-compliance. | Real-time monitoring through integration with telematics devices and GPS sensors, generating automated alerts when temperature fluctuations occur. |
| Extended planning and transit times | Prolonged exposure of food to environmental changes, higher fuel consumption, and risk of missing delivery time windows. | Route planning algorithms that optimize delivery sequences in minutes, reducing miles traveled and transit times. |
| Lack of visibility and unreported incidents | Inability to react promptly to thermograph failures, cooling unit shutdowns, or unnotified delivery delays. | Centralized visibility through a Control Tower, enabling real-time incident management in the field right when issues occur. |
How can you ensure a controlled cold chain with no inventory loss for perishable goods?
Maintaining thermal stability in food products requires shifting from reactive processes to a real-time management ecosystem. In high-demand sectors where time buffers are tight, cold chain continuity is vital to protect brand reputation and customer satisfaction.
How does operational reinforcement protect the HORECA and foodservice industry?
Serving hotels, restaurants, cafeterias (HORECA), and foodservice companies involves inflexible quality requirements. A delay in a delivery window or a thermal variation on the route can ruin high-value perishable items—such as processed meats, dairy, seafood, or pre-formed products—leading to rejection at reception and impacting business continuity. Guaranteeing punctual deliveries within optimal temperature ranges preserves commercial value and prevents direct financial loss.
What is the technical explanation for continuous temperature control ien route?
Technically, continuous temperature control relies on API and webhook integrations between the transport management platform and fleet telematics devices (temperature sensors and GPS systems). This architecture captures constant temperature readings from the cooling or freezing chamber and cross-references them with the vehicle's geographic position. Data is centrally processed within the platform, recording end-to-end shipment traceability from the distribution center to delivery confirmation.
How does the Real-Time Monitoring + Automated Alerts module optimize visibility?
The Real-Time Monitoring + Automated Alerts module serves as a continuous supervision tool. If the internal temperature of a transport unit exceeds the configured threshold for a specific food type, the system immediately sends a notification to both the control center and the driver. This enables dispatch teams to intervene promptly, coordinate cooling unit adjustments, or resequence deliveries before cargo suffers irreversible damage, thereby protecting the food cold chain.
Across Latin America, implementing telematics technology and data integration has allowed major producers to establish safe and efficient operations. A notable example is the Agrosuper success story with Drivin, a market leader with over 65 years of experience producing and marketing poultry, pork, turkey, and processed foods. The company integrated its operating ecosystem with vehicle GPS providers, enabling real-time tracking of location, speed, and temperature across an average of 400 daily vehicles in Chile, significantly strengthening delivery service quality.
Sustaining thermal traceability in food transport is supported by international technical consensus: according to analyses published by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), appropriate cold logistics and management technologies are key to preventing large-scale perishable food losses during transportation and distribution phases in developing regions.
Through these integrated solutions, Descartes + Drivin help companies overcome these challenges, ensuring fresh food logistics operate under the highest standards of control, efficiency, and regulatory compliance.
Evolve from reactive logistics to complete operational control. Speak with our consulting team to evaluate your logistics workflows and discover how to optimize the distribution of your perishable products:

Frecuently asked questions
01. What is the food cold chain and why is it critical?
It is the uninterrupted sequence of storage, handling, and temperature-controlled transportation that preserves perishable products from origin to final delivery. It is critical because it prevents bacterial growth, maintains food nutritional value, and guarantees compliance with food safety regulations.
02. How does a TMS help control the cold chain?
A TMS connected to vehicle telematics and GPS sensors gathers real-time temperature data throughout the route. When a deviation occurs, the software triggers automated alerts so support and incident response teams can take preventive action before cargo is compromised.
03. How are inventory losses reduced in the HORECA industry?
Through route optimization and strict adherence to delivery time windows. Reducing vehicle transit time in the field and avoiding traffic bottlenecks decreases thermal exposure for high-value items destined for restaurants, hotels, and cafes.
04. Is it possible to integrate temperature tracking from different GPS providers?
Yes, a modern TMS platform features API integration capabilities to consolidate location, traffic status, delivery progress, and temperature readings from multiple third-party GPS vendors or thermographs into a single dashboard.

Nagel-Group baut Logistikzentrum für Lebensmittellogistik in Bremen
Visualisierung des neuen Mega-Centers im GVZ Bremen: Der rund 36.650 m² große Neubau wird speziell auf die Anforderungen der Lebensmittellogistik zugeschnitten. Die Fertigstellung ist für Ende 2027 geplant
©Foto: Panattoni
Die Nagel-Group erweitert ihre Kapazitäten in Norddeutschland und errichtet im GVZ Bremen ein neues Logistikzentrum für die Lebensmittellogistik. Der 36.650 Quadratmeter große Neubau soll Ende 2027 fertiggestellt werden.
von Deborah Baran
Kommentare
Teilen

 #Nagel Group
 #Logistikzentrum
 #Lebensmitteltransport
Die Nagel-Group erweitert ihr Standortnetzwerk in Deutschland mit einem neuen Logistikzentrum im Güterverkehrszentrum (GVZ) Bremen. Der auf die Lebensmittellogistik zugeschnittene Neubau entsteht auf einem rund 90.510 Quadratmeter großen Grundstück und wird vom Industrie-, Logistik- und Gewerbeimmobilienentwickler Panattoni entwickelt und realisiert. Die Bauarbeiten sollen im Oktober 2026 beginnen. Die Fertigstellung und Übergabe des Standorts sind für Dezember 2027 geplant.
„Das neue Logistikzentrum in Bremen ist eine Investition in die Zukunft der Lebensmittellogistik. Der neue Standort wird modernste Logistikprozesse mit einem nachhaltigen Energiekonzept verbinden und schafft die Voraussetzungen für weiteres Wachstum. Gleichzeitig entstehen moderne Arbeitsplätze in einer der wichtigsten Logistikregionen Deutschlands“, erläutert Lars-Erik Poths, CEO der Nagel-Group.
Neuer Food-Standort mit 36.650 Quadratmetern Fläche
Das Logistikzentrum wird insgesamt rund 36.650 Quadratmeter Nutzfläche umfassen. Geplant sind etwa 29.500 Quadratmeter Hallenfläche, 5.200 Quadratmeter Büro- und Sozialflächen sowie 1.950 Quadratmeter Mezzaninfläche.
Die Immobilie wird speziell für die Anforderungen der Lebensmittellogistik ausgelegt. Vorgesehen sind ein Cross-Dock-Terminal sowie temperaturgeführte Bereiche für Ambient-, Frische- und Ultrafrische-Produkte. Darüber hinaus entstehen ein viergeschossiger Bürotrakt, eine Lkw-Werkstatt mit Waschstraße, eine Tankstelle sowie Ladeinfrastruktur für Lkw, Pkw und Fahrräder.
Am Standort sollen künftig rund 400 Arbeitsplätze geschaffen werden, darunter etwa 20 Ausbildungsplätze.
Nachhaltiges Energiekonzept mit Photovoltaik und Speicher
Ein zentraler Bestandteil der Planung ist nach Angaben des Unternehmens die nachhaltige Energieversorgung des Standorts. Vorgesehen sind Photovoltaikanlagen in Kombination mit einem Stromspeicher, der den erzeugten Solarstrom zwischenspeichert und bedarfsgerecht bereitstellt.
Die Wärme- und Kälteversorgung soll vollständig ohne fossile Energieträger erfolgen. Dafür ist eine moderne Heiz- und Kälteanlage mit integrierter Gebäudeleittechnik vorgesehen. Für den Neubau werde zudem eine DGNB-Gold-Zertifizierung angestrebt.
Nagel-Group und Panattoni entwickeln Build-to-suit-Projekt
Das Logistikzentrum wird als maßgeschneidertes Build-to-suit-Projekt realisiert. Nach Angaben der Projektpartner erfolgte die Entwicklung des Konzepts in enger Zusammenarbeit zwischen Nagel-Group und Panattoni.
„Das Projekt zeigt, wie wichtig der partnerschaftliche Austausch aller Beteiligten ist. Bereits in einer frühen Planungsphase konnten wir gemeinsam mit der Nagel-Group ein Konzept entwickeln, das optimal auf ihre Anforderungen zugeschnitten ist und zugleich hohe wirtschaftliche sowie nachhaltige Standards erfüllt“, sagt Fred-Markus Bohne, Managing Partner Panattoni DACH & Nordics.
GVZ Bremen bietet trimodale Verkehrsanbindung
Das GVZ Bremen ist ein bedeutender Logistikstandort Europas: Der Standort verfügt über eine trimodale Anbindung über Straße, Schiene und Wasser. In unmittelbarer Nähe liegen die Autobahnen A281, A1 und A27 sowie der Flughafen Bremen. Zudem bestehen Anbindungen an die Seehäfen Bremerhaven, Wilhelmshaven und Hamburg. Damit bietet das GVZ Bremen gute Voraussetzungen für nationale und internationale Warenströme.
Mit dem Neubau will die Nagel-Group ihren Kurs zur Modernisierung und Weiterentwicklung ihres europäischen Standortnetzwerks fortsetzen und zusätzliche Kapazitäten für die Lebensmittellogistik schaffen.

Fiege: Weiteres Logistikzentrum für Pharma-Branche in Münster
News vom 12.08.2026 von Anna Barbara Brüggmann
Logistikdienstleister Fiege erweitert die Kapazitäten am Standort Münster-Hessenweg: Neben dem bestehenden Healthcare-Logistikzentrum wird ein Single-User-Center mit über 10.000 Quadratmetern Logistikfläche errichtet.
Eigenen Angaben zufolge errichtet Fiege eine weitere Logistikanlage im Gewerbegebiet Münster-Hessenweg. In unmittelbarer Nachbarschaft zum bestehenden Healthcare-Standort sei ein Neubau geplant, der speziell auf die Anforderungen der Pharmabranche ausgelegt ist.
9.800 Quadratmeter Logistikfläche
Der Baustart ist für August 2026, die Fertigstellung für Juni 2027 vorgesehen. Als Standortvorteile nennt das Unternehmen die verkehrsgünstige Anbindung sowie die Nähe zu pharmazeutischen Produktionsstandorten
Die Immobilie wird von Fiege Real Estate entwickelt. Das Gebäude umfasse circa 9.800 Quadratmeter Logistikfläche, mehr als 1.000 Quadratmeter Mezzaninfläche sowie einen 430 Quadratmeter großen Bürobereich.
Zur Energieeffizienz beitragen sollen LED-Beleuchtung und eine Luft-Luft-Wärmepumpe. Vorgesehen sei auch eine Ladeinfrastruktur mit 200-Kilowatt-Leistung für E-Lkw sowie eine PV-Anlage mit einer Leistung von rund 1.000 Kilowatt-Peak auf dem Dach.
Diese soll einen wesentlichen Teil des Strombedarfs vor Ort erzeugen. Zudem sei die technische Infrastruktur für eine mögliche Erweiterung ausgelegt.
Der Logistikdienstleister strebt den Angaben zufolge eine Gold-Zertifizierung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Nachhaltiges Bauen (DGNB) für den Neubau an.
Ausbau der Kapazitäten
Laut Jens Fiege, Co-CEO der Fiege-Gruppe, ist das Unternehmen seit einigen Jahren am Standort Münster-Hessenweg vertreten und wickelt die Logistik für verschiedene Unternehmen aus der Gesundheitsbranche ab.
„Wir freuen uns, dass wir hier eine weitere, hochmoderne Immobilie errichten und unsere Kapazitäten ausbauen können“, erklärt Jens Fiege. Er fügt hinzu: „Mit dem zusätzlichen Logistikzentrum schaffen wir nun die Voraussetzungen, um unsere Kunden aus dem Healthcare-Bereich noch flexibler zu unterstützen und weiteres Wachstum zu ermöglichen.“

Fiege: Fünf neue E-Lkw – Flotte wächst auf 25 elektrische Trucks
News vom 05.08.2026 von Daniela Sawary-Kohnen
Der Grevener Logistiker stockt seinen elektrifizierten Fuhrpark um fünf neue Mercedes-Benz eActros 600 auf. Sie sollen die Niederlassungen Rangsdorf und Bremen verstärken.
Fiege treibt die Elektrifizierung seiner E-Lkw-Flotte für den emissionsfreien Transport im Fernverkehr weiter voran und hat vergangene Woche im Wörther Werk von Mercedes-Benz fünf neue Sattelzugmaschinen vom Typ eActros 600 in Empfang genommen.
Christian Thiemann, Managing Director der Fiege-Geschäftseinheit Transport:
„Der Verkehrs- und Transportsektor ist nach wie vor einer der größten Emissionstreiber in Deutschland und verfehlt die Klimaziele bislang deutlich. Deshalb ist die fortschreitende Dekarbonisierung unseres Fuhrparks eine zentrale Säule unserer Nachhaltigkeitsstrategie. Wir möchten unsere CO2e-Emissionen stetig reduzieren und unserer Verantwortung als Logistikdienstleister gerecht werden. Die neuen E-Lkw helfen uns, das Thema emissionsfreie Transporte gemeinsam mit unseren Kunden weiter voranzutreiben.“
Drei LFP-Batteriepakete
Drei LFP-Batteriepakete mit einer Gesamtkapazität von rund 621 Kilowattstunden sorgten dafür, dass die vollelektrischen Fahrzeuge über eine Reichweite von bis zu 500 Kilometern ohne Nachladen verfügten, heißt es weiter. Die zusätzlichen eActros 600, mit denen Fiege die Zahl der schweren E-Lkw in seiner internationalen Flotte auf 25 erhöht, werden an den Niederlassungen in Rangsdorf und Bremen eingesetzt.
In Deutschland hat der Logistiker bereits 17 schwere E-Lkw der Marken Mercedes-Benz, Volvo und Designwerk im Einsatz. Im Laufe des Augusts soll noch ein MAN eGTX für den Standort Unna hinzukommen. Christian Thiemann:
„Um die Fahrzeuge so flexibel wie möglich nutzen zu können, investieren wir an unseren Niederlassungen flächendeckend in den Ausbau der Ladeinfrastruktur. In Deutschland haben wir mittlerweile 20 Schnellladepunkte installiert, bis Ende des Jahres werden es 30 sein.“
In der Schweiz verfügt Fiege zudem aktuell über acht batterieelektrische schwere Lkw, für die am Standort Oftringen im Kanton Aargau kürzlich ein eigener E-Ladepark eröffnet wurde.

Fiege: Fulfillment für Hautpflegemarke Nø Cosmetics
News vom 28.07.2026 von Daniela Sawary-Kohnen
Der Logistiker ist neuer Kooperationspartner von der Conscious-Beauty-Brand aus Dormagen und wickelt hierfür in seiner Niederlassung in Emmerich das Kontraktgeschäft ab.
Der Kontraktlogistiker Fiege unterstützt die Hautpflegemarke Nø Cosmetic bei seiner neuen Wachstumsstrategie. Für das B2B- und B2C-Fulfillment übernimmt der Logistiker damit an seinem Standort in Emmerich neben Lagerlogistik auch individuelle Mehrwertdienstleistungen sowie Verpackung und Versand von Bestellungen aus Onlinehandel und Retail. David Bothe, Managing Director der Fiege-Geschäftseinheit Consumer Goods:
„Als internationaler Logistikdienstleister mit jahrzehntelanger Erfahrung in der FMCG-Branche kennen wir die speziellen Anforderungen im Beauty-Bereich sehr genau. Um B2B- und B2C-Fulfillment zuverlässig abwickeln und saisonalen Schwankungen schnell und erfolgreich begegnen zu können, ist hohe Flexibilität gefragt. Mit unserem eingespielten Team, der Multi-User-Struktur unseres Standortes im Emmerich und unseren maßgeschneiderten Transportlösungen können wir die erforderliche Anpassungsfähigkeit jederzeit gewährleisten. Wir sind dankbar, dass uns Nø Cosmetics das Vertrauen schenkt – und freuen uns auf die Zusammenarbeit.“
Unterstützung des TikTok-Shops
Das 2017 gegründete Unternehmen Nø Cosmetics hat sich in den vergangenen Jahren von einem Start-up zu einem etablierten Anbieter hochwertiger und veganer Clean-Beauty-Produkte entwickelt.
Vertrieben wird das Sortiment über eine breit angelegte Multi-Channel-Strategie. Neben dem eigenen Onlineshop sind die tierversuchsfreien Produkte in zwei eigenen Stores sowie bei allen führenden Drogeriemärkten in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz erhältlich.
Zusätzlich zur Logistikabwicklung hat Fiege das Unternehmen nach eigenen Angaben auch beim Launch des eigenen TikTok-Shops unterstützt. Caroline Kroll, CEO und Co-Gründerin von Nø Cosmetics:
„Die Nachfrage nach innovativer, hochwertiger und bezahlbarer Hautpflege steigt rasant, weshalb unsere Skincare-Brand in den vergangenen Jahren ein starkes Wachstum verzeichnet hat. Als logische Folge haben wir unsere bestehenden Fulfillment-Strukturen überdacht und

Maersk hat in Herleshausen in Mitteldeutschland ein neues Logistikzentrum eröffnet. Der Standort verfügt über knapp 72.000 Quadratmeter Fläche und kann während der Hochsaison im E-Commerce bis zu 1.000 Beschäftigte aufnehmen.

Maersk
Dieser Text wurde mit Unterstützung eines automatischen Übersetzungstools erstellt. Es kann daher zu inhaltlichen und sprachlichen Ungenauigkeiten kommen. Vielen Dank für Ihr Verständnis.
Das Logistikzentrum im Panattoni Park Bad Hersfeld Ost in Hessen lagert bereits seit August Waren ein. Inzwischen ist auch der Versand angelaufen: Von Herleshausen aus werden Produkte an die Verteilzentren eines nicht näher genannten Onlinehändlers versandt.
Insgesamt umfasst der Standort 71.800 Quadratmeter Logistikfläche. Davon entfallen 62.800 Quadratmeter auf Lagerflächen, 6.100 Quadratmeter auf Zwischengeschosse und 2.900 Quadratmeter auf Bürobereiche. Maersk hat das Gebäude langfristig angemietet.
Durch die direkte Lage an der Autobahn A4 ist das Logistikzentrum an eine der wichtigsten Ost-West-Verbindungen Deutschlands angebunden. Zudem befindet es sich in der Nähe des geografischen Zentrums der Bundesrepublik.
> Herleshausen ist der ideale Standort für einen zentralen Knotenpunkt des Warenverkehrs innerhalb Deutschlands und in die benachbarten europäischen Märkte, erklärte Ole Trumpfheller, Geschäftsführer der Maersk Area Northern Europe Continent.
Maersk rechnet im Regelbetrieb mit 300 bis 400 festen Arbeitsplätzen. In der Hochsaison von Oktober bis Dezember könnte die Zahl der Beschäftigten jedoch auf bis zu 1.000 steigen.
Zum Zeitpunkt der Eröffnungsankündigung waren bereits rund 150 Menschen am Standort beschäftigt. Die Suche nach weiteren Arbeitskräften läuft weiter.
Das Gebäude verfügt über Solarmodule, Anlagen zur Regenwassernutzung und Ladeinfrastruktur für Elektrofahrzeuge. Darüber hinaus strebt Maersk für den Standort eine Gold-Zertifizierung der Deutschen Gesellschaft für Nachhaltiges Bauen (DGNB) an.

Amazon Deutschland: Newsübersicht zu aktuellen Entwicklungen in E-Commerce, Logistik und Innovationen
Amazon Deutschland treibt Innovation und Expansion gezielt voran – mit neuen Logistikzentren in Dummerstorf, Horn-Bad Meinberg und Sachsen-Anhalt, Same Day Delivery, KI-Rechenzentren und nachhaltiger Verpackung. Der Online-Riese setzt auf Elektromobilität, Robotik mit Tastsinn und strategische Partnerschaften wie mit Knuspr. Über 4.000 neue Jobs, 15 Millionen entfernte Fälschungen und Investitionen in Höhe von zehn Milliarden Euro zeigen: Amazon bleibt Motor für den E-Commerce und die Logistik in Deutschland.

Indre-et-Loire : un nouvel entrepôt réfrigéré pour Danone, à Sorigny
Engagé à l’été 2025, après la signature d’un BEFA (bail en l’état futur d’achèvement), le projet est désormais achevé. Cette nouvelle implantation, stratégique pour la région, est située à proximité des autoroutes A10 et A85, à une quinzaine de kilomètres au sud de Tours.
La zone d’activités accueille plus de 1 400 salariés et totalise près de 100 000 m² de surfaces logistiques. Le btiment développe une superficie de 8 200 m², dont 6 400 m² sont consacrés au stockage sous froid positif (entre 2 et 6 °C). Il est équipé d’une centrale photovoltaïque en toiture de près de 3 000 m², affichant une puissance de 580 kWc et destinée à l’autoconsommation.
Le dispositif est complété par des batteries d’une capacité de 230 kWh, conçues pour optimiser l’autoconsommation énergétique. Labellisé Aut0nom®, l’entrepôt devrait permettre de réduire de 35 % les émissions de CO₂ du site. Argan et Danone sont liés par un bail ferme de neuf ans.
À terme, cette nouvelle plateforme remplacera progressivement l’ancien entrepôt frigorifique de Danone situé à Chambray-lès-Tours.

Sécurité alimentaire : la DFC finance un entrepôt de 10 000 palettes
Mercredi 22 Juillet 2026 - 13:05
L'ambassade des États-Unis au Sénégal a pris part, lundi, à la pose de la première pierre d'un nouvel entrepôt frigorifique destiné à la chaîne alimentaire. Financée par la DFC américaine en partenariat avec IFRIA, l'infrastructure offrira 10 000 palettes de stockage et plus de 200 emplois.
Sécurité alimentaire : la DFC finance un entrepôt de 10 000 palettes Sécurité alimentaire : la DFC finance un entrepôt de 10 000 palettes "Sécurité alimentaire : la DFC finance un entrepôt de 10 000 palettes")
Cette cérémonie a marqué le lancement des travaux d'une plateforme logistique conçue pour combler l'une des faiblesses structurelles de l'agriculture sénégalaise : la conservation des denrées entre la récolte et leur mise sur le marché. Le financement de ce chantier provient de la Société américaine de financement du développement international, mieux connue sous son sigle DFC, associée pour ce projet à l'entreprise IFRIA, chargée de sa réalisation opérationnelle sur le terrain.   
Une fois achevé, l'entrepôt sera en mesure d'accueillir jusqu'à 10 000 palettes de marchandises, un volume qui doit permettre d'absorber une part significative des productions locales en attente de distribution. Le chantier devrait également générer plus de 200 emplois directs, principalement au bénéfice des communautés environnantes, dans un secteur logistique où la main-d'œuvre qualifiée reste encore insuffisamment développée à l'échelle nationale.   
Au-delà du simple stockage, l'objectif affiché par les partenaires du projet consiste à consolider la sécurité alimentaire du pays en limitant les pertes survenant après les récoltes, un phénomène qui continue de peser lourdement sur les revenus des producteurs sénégalais. L'amélioration de la chaîne logistique agricole figure également parmi les retombées attendues, la nouvelle infrastructure devant fluidifier la circulation des produits entre les zones de production et les marchés de consommation. Cette ambition rejoint celle d'autres grands chantiers agroalimentaires récemment engagés dans le pays, à l'image de la raffinerie d'huiles alimentaires inaugurée à Sendou, pensée elle aussi pour réduire la dépendance du Sénégal aux importations et renforcer sa capacité de transformation locale.   
Du côté des autorités américaines, on met en avant la dimension régionale du projet, cet entrepôt devant renforcer la place du Sénégal comme carrefour logistique pour l'ensemble de la sous-région, en facilitant à la fois l'entreposage et l'acheminement des produits agricoles vers d'autres marchés. Cette initiative s'inscrit dans le cadre plus large de la coopération américano-sénégalaise en matière d'investissements agricoles et de développement des échanges commerciaux, un partenariat qui vient compléter les efforts déjà engagés par l'État sénégalais lui-même pour sécuriser le financement de son secteur primaire, notamment à travers une opération de titrisation de 80 milliards de francs CFA destinée à garantir un accès plus souple au crédit pour les intrants et le matériel agricole.   
Pour les agriculteurs, entreprises et communautés locales situés dans la zone d'implantation, ce nouvel équipement devrait ouvrir des perspectives concrètes : de meilleures conditions de conservation des récoltes, un recul sensible des pertes de production et de nouveaux débouchés en matière d'emploi une fois l'infrastructure opérationnelle.
